rows.en: The root of this compromise between the statements that contradict one another is not a new invention of ours; rather it is the opinion of the sages of the Talmud, if we read their words with attention. Behold, the masters of the Talmud from of old held dear every single thing that one of the sages would newly bring forth, if it was upright and true in their eyes; they so exalted the worth of that thing that it was counted in their eyes as though it had been given at Sinai. And this is said explicitly in the Talmud (Yerushalmi Sanhedrin 6:1; Sifre Ekev, piska 41): "'They are given from one shepherd' [Ecclesiastes 12:11]. The Holy One, blessed be He, said: If you have heard [a word of Torah] from the mouth of a small one in Israel and it pleased you, let it not be in your eyes as one who hears from the mouth of a small one, but as one who heard it from the mouth of a great one; and not as one who heard it from the mouth of a great one, but as one who heard it from the mouth of a sage; and not as one who heard it from the mouth of a sage, but as one who heard it from the mouth of a prophet; and not as one who heard it from the mouth of a prophet, but as one who heard it from the mouth of the shepherd, and 'shepherd' is none other than Moses." The idea that looks out from this statement, only by a light hint, is set out very clearly and with understanding in the words of one of the later sages (*Tanna de-Vei Eliyahu*), who said: "Whoever brings forth new words of Torah by his own mouth is like one whom they make to hear from heaven." And the masters of the aggadah depict this idea in a pictorial figure of speech. In describing the greatness of R. Akiva they said (Menaḥot 29b): "The Holy One, blessed be He, showed Moses R. Akiva, who was sitting and expounding, and Moses did not know what he was saying, and Moses' strength failed, until he came to one matter of the Torah and his disciples asked him: From where do you have this? And he said: It is a halakhah [given] to Moses at Sinai. At once his mind was set at rest." Behold, in this parable the speaker portrays the midrashim that the middle generations of the Tannaim expounded, and especially the generation of R. Akiva, of whom it was said that he expounded heaps upon heaps of halakhot on every single tittle of the Torah. Do we not see eye to eye that in his opinion all these midrashim were new, lately come from the minds of those who said and expounded them, which their forebears had not imagined, so that Moses himself was astonished that the features of his Torah were changed: he did not recognize his words and did not know his statutes, because the interpretations had changed their sense, and for this reason his strength failed? But his mind was quickly set at rest when he saw that the expounded matters were hung on a halakhah [given] to Moses at Sinai (Jellinek, in his sermons).⚠1 And now, who will not recognize from this aggadah that the ancients did not take the expression "a halakhah [given] to Moses at Sinai" with exactness and precision, but, as we have said, they said it even of new matters, since in their opinion all the new interpretations lay within the statute of the Torah? Therefore they could rightly say of R. Akiva and his colleagues: "Things that were not revealed to Moses were revealed to R. Akiva and his colleagues" (Numbers Rabbah 19). And one of the sages of the Talmud, R. Abbahu, reveals to us the secret of the matter when he says: "Did Moses then learn the whole Torah? It is written: 'The measure thereof is longer than the earth, and broader than the sea' [Job 11:9], and in forty days Moses learned it? Rather, the Holy One, blessed be He, taught him general rules" (Exodus Rabbah 41). We do not wish here to expound and inquire which general rules the speaker meant by this; but this much comes out clearly from his words: that in his opinion the Holy One, blessed be He, left the unfolding of the intent of the Torah to the sages, and nothing was handed to Moses except the general rules of the Oral Torah. True, this will seem a wonder in the eyes of the believers who walk in their simplicity and are used to believing things as they stand and as they are written; but it is not too wonderful nor far off, if the matters are examined with attention. For from of old they believed that the Torah itself gave them a great license to expound and interpret its words, and by the power of this license their midrashim rose to the rank that belongs to things stated explicitly in the Torah. This license they found in the saying of the Torah: "Thou shalt not turn aside from the sentence which they shall declare unto thee (the priests the Levites, or the judge that shall be in those days), to the right hand, nor to the left" (Deuteronomy 17:10)⚠2: "even if they tell you of the right that it is the left" (Sifre, Shofetim). And the strength of their faith in this authorization is described in their saying (Rosh Hashanah 25b): "You have only the court that is in your own days." And they said of several conditions of the commandments and their limits, whose mark is not seen in the Torah, that "Scripture handed them over to the sages" (Ḥagigah 18b; Bekhorot 26b; Sifre Re'eh, piska 135). This handing over includes the power of the sages to judge and to rule according to their wisdom and their understanding, and it is well described by the author of the introduction to *Halakhot Gedolot*, who expounded the verse "according to the law which they shall teach thee" [Deuteronomy 17:11] and noted from its wording that it does not say "which she shall teach thee" but "which they shall teach thee": this teaches that one is obliged to listen to the sages who will be in those days in all that they teach from their wisdom, even if their teaching is not explicit in the Written Torah. And without doubt this too is the sense of their saying "Scripture handed them over to the sages." And since the Torah itself gave them this license, all their interpretations and expositions had the rank of things given at Sinai; therefore it will no longer seem a wonder to us if they call even the interpretations that are new or doubtful, as to their origin and the time of their founding, by the name "interpretations of Sinai." It is already well known how precious and honored this license was in their eyes, so that even the commandments of the sages were with them in some measure like the commandments of the Torah, and they did not hold back from instituting blessings over them and framing the blessings in the form of those over the commandments written in the Torah, saying: "who has sanctified us with His commandments and commanded us to do such and such," as with the commandments of the sages (Shabbat 23b). Yet if we ask: how is it possible that a new interpretation should be ascribed to tradition? And what does it help us to say that by the power of the license the Torah gave them all their interpretations and novellae rose to the rank of the things said at Sinai? Even so, it is not fitting to call them by the name of the things given at Sinai in defiance of the truth! And how can our reason bear to say that men of truth and men of faith such as those sages would say plainly of all the interpretations that they are from Sinai, when they knew in their hearts that for the most part they were new, from the sages of each generation? To these questions we will find no answer unless we say that they believed that in all that the Scribes interpreted, and the sages, the masters of the midrash of the Torah who came after them, they were helped by divine help to agree in their interpretations with the original intent that lies in the words of the Written Torah. Many statements of the sages of the Talmud hint at the belief that God gave wisdom to the expounders to find the right intent in the Torah, in agreement with the original intent, and they said explicitly (Sifre Pinḥas, piska 134) that the Torah gave understanding to the sages to expound and to teach. So too they said of Joshua (Yerushalmi Pe'ah 8, and in many places): "Even things that he had not heard from his master, his mind agreed with what was said to Moses at Sinai." From the content of this statement we learn that the masters of the Talmud held that not everything said to Moses at Sinai did he hand on to Joshua; for otherwise, how had Joshua not heard from his master what had been said to him at Sinai? And this agrees with what one of the later sages of the Torah said (*Tosafot Yom Tov*, in his introduction): that what the Holy One, blessed be He, showed Moses, the fine points of the Torah and the fine points of the Scribes, this Moses did not hand on to others at all. And on the second side we learn from it that they believed that through faithful exposition the expounder comes to agree with the original intent, for the Torah gives him understanding to expound and to teach. And the aggadah tells (Temurah 16a) of the greatness of Othniel son of Kenaz, who by his dialectic restored a great number of the halakhot that had been forgotten in the days of mourning for Moses. The inner idea of this aggadah too hints at their belief in the divine help that is with those who devote themselves to expounding the Torah, until they come to agree with the original intent. For otherwise, how could they say that he restored the forgotten halakhot? If they had been forgotten, who told them that what Othniel brought out by his dialectic truly agreed with the forgotten ones? Necessarily we must picture this aggadah thus: there were halakhot that were doubtful to them and they did not know what Moses had said about them, and Othniel son of Kenaz came and expounded the Torah until he quieted the doubts, and they believed that his mind had agreed with what was said to Moses at Sinai. And this aggadah is not alone of its kind; for likewise we are told (Genesis Rabbah 72; Song of Songs Rabbah on "Thou art beautiful, O my love, as Tirzah" [Song of Songs 6:4]): "The tribe of Issachar would set up two hundred heads of Sanhedrins, and all their brethren would agree on the halakhah according to them, and it would answer them halakhah as the halakhah [given] to Moses at Sinai." Now although all these stories have only the value of aggadah, yet one thing comes out from all of them, and it is this: that they believed that all the new expositions were in their eyes as though received from Sinai and were called by them by the name "tradition from Sinai," because they believed that their minds agreed with what was said at Sinai, and that by their dialectic they aimed at the original intent.

1.note: Reference to Jellinek's sermons as printed, with no title or page; kept as given.

2.note: Printed 17, 10; the quoted words 'thou shalt not turn aside ... to the right hand, nor to the left' are Deuteronomy 17:11.

rows.en: But this view, that they believed their minds agreed with the original intent, is possible only where the expounded matter is agreed by all, with none disputing it at any time. But if we pass over the field of the midrashim of the sages, we find that many times the law was decided by one court on the basis of the midrash of the Torah, and another court came after it and decided the law the opposite of the first, and its decision too was taken from the midrash of the Torah. Now how is it possible that both should agree with the original intent, when they expound from one extreme to the opposite? And not only did this happen by chance; rather it was an agreed rule with them that a later court has the power to decide a matter on the basis of the midrash of the Torah the opposite of what the court before it had decided, even though that court's decision too was correct and founded on the midrash of the Torah (Maimonides, Laws of Rebels, chapter 2, from the Talmud). And at various times this truly happened. Already in the period of the Scribes and immediately after them we find traces of this. For instance, the prohibition they observed against fighting on the Sabbath: this custom is very old. In the days of Ptolemy Lagi, who reigned in Alexandria after the death of Alexander the Macedonian, Jerusalem was taken on the Sabbath, because the Jews rested on the Sabbath and for this reason did not stand against the conqueror (Josephus, *Antiquities*, part 2, book 12, chapter 1).⚠1 And some time later, in the days of the Hasmonean war, this prohibition was still well known; for in the days of Mattathias the Hasmonean, although they fought their enemies with zeal beyond compare, the holiness of the Sabbath nevertheless kept them from fighting on the Sabbath (Josephus, ibid., chapter 6; First Book of Maccabees, chapter 2). And even when they took counsel together and agreed to permit the matter, they permitted it only for the hour; for so it is told that when Pompey the Roman went up against Jerusalem and took the city, it was easy for him to take it because of the Sabbath day, which is the day on which the Jews refrain from fighting (Josephus, ibid., book 14, chapter 2).⚠2 Now we have seen that even at the time when they acted permissively in this, they did so only out of necessity, but they did not interpret the statute of the Torah in this direction. Yet we see that some time later Shammai the Elder came and permitted fighting on the Sabbath, not out of necessity alone or for the need of the hour, but on the basis of the law of the Torah, relying on his midrash, in which he expounded "until it fall" [Deuteronomy 20:20]: "even on the Sabbath" (Shabbat 18a;⚠3 and Sifre, Shofetim). So too we find in the matter of field labor in the seventh year, that at one time they forbade a kind of labor and based the prohibition on Scripture, and at the time after it they permitted it, likewise relying on Scripture; and the sages of the Talmud said this explicitly (Yerushalmi Shevi'it 1:1): "When they forbade, they relied on Scripture, and when they permitted, they relied on Scripture." And close to this they said in another place (Genesis Rabbah, parashah 82): "And what did they see to keep at a distance and to bring near? They read a verse and kept at a distance; they read a verse and brought near." Now, the matter being so, how is it possible to hold the view we mentioned, that they believed their minds agreed, in their exposition, with the original intent, when we see that one court decides a matter and another court decides its opposite? How can we justify both and say of them that both spoke rightly and both aimed at the original intent? But although it is true that one cannot suppose two opposite views in the intent of some statement and say that the speaker meant both together, nevertheless this was not wondrous and far-fetched in the eyes of the sages of the Talmud, because they held a great rule in which they believed: that the Giver of the Torah designed it so from the beginning, that the words of the Torah should be fit to be interpreted in different ways and should bear opposite interpretations, to declare unclean and also clean, to forbid and also to permit, and that the prohibition and the permission, the uncleanness and the cleanness, should lie together within the statute of the Torah and its intent. And so it would not seem a wonder in their eyes if one utterance in the Torah were interpreted by one court as a prohibition and the same utterance interpreted by a later court as a permission; for they could say of the two interpretations that both lay within the intent of the Torah, and that the minds of both agreed with the original intent, which was said, or handed over, or hinted, or made known in its general rules to Moses. Such was truly and clearly the view of the sages of the Oral Torah. And they said explicitly: "With every single utterance the Holy One, blessed be He, told Moses forty-nine ways [of declaring] clean and forty-nine ways [of declaring] unclean" (Song of Songs Rabbah on "He brought me" [Song of Songs 2:4]); and they exalted the greatness of the sages who knew how to expound the Torah according to these opposite ways (Eruvin 13b). Therefore the court of each and every time, which judged according to what seemed to it the intent of the Torah, its mind agreed with what was said to Moses at Sinai, whether it judged to permit or to forbid, whether for uncleanness or for cleanness. And one of the sages depicts this matter in a pleasing image (Yerushalmi Sanhedrin 9:2):⚠4 "Had the Torah been given cut [and dried] (fixed in its laws), there would be no standing for the foot (that is, the thing would have no lasting existence). What is the reason? 'And the Lord spoke unto Moses.' He said before Him: Master of the world, let me know how the halakhah is. He said to him: 'To incline after the many' [Exodus 23:2], so that the Torah may be expounded in forty-nine ways clean and in forty-nine ways unclean." Behold, this speaker pictures in his mind as though the Holy One, blessed be He, showed Moses all the possible ways of interpreting the Torah, a thing and its opposite, whether to forbid or to permit, for uncleanness and for cleanness. And Moses wonders at this: how is it possible that the Torah should be interpreted in ways that differ and oppose one another? And he longs to know which ways are according to the truth and according to the halakhah. To this the Holy One, blessed be He, answers him that this is handed over to the sages of the generations, and when the majority of those standing for the count agree on one side, then that will be counted the halakhah and the truth. And He also tells him the reason: that it is a necessity for the endurance of the Torah that it be fit to be interpreted in ways to declare clean and in ways to declare unclean. Another of the sages of the Talmud followed this idea too (Tosefta Sotah 7; Ḥagigah 3b), who said: "The Torah is likened to a planting: as a planting is fruitful and multiplies, so the words of the Torah are fruitful and multiply." Words as clear as these need no explanation. Now although most of these proofs are taken from words of aggadah, and the manner of the images on this matter is not the same in all of them, nevertheless it is agreed that in one respect aggadot like these are faithful witnesses, which bear witness to the features of the beliefs and opinions that ruled in the nation at the time of their founding; and in the matter before us they bear witness to the character of the opinions that spread among the Jews with regard to the Oral Torah. And it becomes clear to us from them that they believed: that many interpretations and halakhot were received by tradition; many were forgotten in the course of time and in the wanderings of the nation, and the sages of the generations restored them from their own understanding and reasoning and by their dialectic, with divine help, until they agreed with the original intent. And also many interpretations and halakhot were newly made and were with them as though received, because the belief in the power of the authorization that the Torah had given them was strong in their hearts. And also when they sometimes turned aside from the way in which their forebears had walked in interpreting the Torah, they relied on the great foundation in which they believed: that this lies in the wisdom of the Giver of the Torah, not to give the Torah cut and fixed; rather, His intent was that the Torah should be fruitful and multiply like a planting, and the heads of the generations in all times were authorized by the authorization of the Torah to interpret it as their eyes and their reason saw fit. And they decided the law that came out of the force of their exposition and inquiry according to the agreement of the majority. And the agreement of the majority was for them a measure for each and every time, to establish halakhah for practice, for "you have only the court that is in your own days." And both when they forbade and when they permitted, they based the matter on Scripture, and this was no lessening of the statute of truth, for they believed that the Torah was given in forty-nine ways clean and in forty-nine ways unclean. These are the beliefs and opinions of the ancients, the masters of the Talmud; and therefore our spirit will be at rest and every doubt will depart if we see a great opposition between the sense of some statutes in the most ancient time, in all the days of the prophets and the exile, and their sense in a late time, in the days of the sages of the Talmud; or if we see that even in this late time not all the generations are alike in understanding the Torah; for according to their opinion and their belief, "these and these are the words of the living God."

1.note: Printed so; Ptolemy's taking of Jerusalem on the Sabbath is Antiquities 12.1.1 ('ח"ב' is perhaps the volume of the edition used).

2.note: Pompey's capture of Jerusalem is in Antiquities 14.4; kept as printed.

3.note: Image reads י"ח.; Shammai's exposition 'until it fall, even on the Sabbath' is in Shabbat 19a.

4.note: Image reads פ"ט ה"ב; the passage is in Yerushalmi Sanhedrin 4:2. Kept as printed.

rows.en: Simeon the Just, one of the last of the Men of the Great Assembly.

Reports of particulars of the Oral Torah that are children of the first period have not reached us in writing; and what has been told us about them is the utterance of later writers, and we do not know which of their reports rests on tradition and which comes from conjecture. And we should not wonder at the lack of clear early reports on matters of the Torah: even of the sources of the nation's history in general from ancient days only poor and scanty remnants have reached us. And had not one of our honored priests at the end of the days of the Temple, namely Josephus Flavius, called Josephus the Priest, left us in writing in a book precious remnants of the history of our people, of our antiquities and of the wars of the Lord that were fought against the enemies of Israel, then the history of the whole period of the Second Temple would have been forgotten and every memory of it lost.{v1_05_12:1} Yet of the times after their return from the exile, while they were still under the rule of the last Persian kings, even he could not report their history. And even the one incident that he tells (*Antiquities*, book 12, chapter 6)⚠1 of what happened in the days of Artaxerxes II (about the year of the world 3628), of the quarrel between two brothers who were priests, is only a small thing for the history of the nation. But for the work before us it is right for us nonetheless to mention it here, as it gives a little light on the religious situation at that time. Jehoiada son of Eliashib died, and his son Joḥanan served as high priest in his place, in the reign of the Persian king Artaxerxes II (about the year of the world 3628). The king's general was Bagoas. He was governor of the province of Syria and Tyre, and the Land of Israel too was under his command. This governor had a friend named Jeshua, the brother of Joḥanan the high priest. Jeshua envied his brother, and his eye and his heart were always on the high priesthood. This longing of his was strengthened by the governor's love for him and by the promise the governor had made him to take the high priesthood away from his brother Joḥanan and to make him priest in his place. This promise emboldened Jeshua, until he began to stir up a quarrel with his brother and went up to Jerusalem to carry out his plot. And it came to pass one day, when both of them were in the Temple and quarreled with one another, that Joḥanan rose up in his anger and killed his brother in the Temple of the Lord. When Bagoas heard of the abomination that had been done in Israel and in the Sanctuary of the Lord, he hastened to go up to Jerusalem to investigate what had been done. When he came there he wished to enter the Sanctuary of the Lord, but the priests wanted to prevent him, for it is a statute in Israel that no foreigner may enter the Temple. Then his anger was kindled against them greatly, and he said: "Is this one, who murdered a human being in the Temple, purer than I?" And he entered by force. Then he laid a penalty on the Temple, that they should pay fifty drachmas for every lamb offered on the altar of the Lord. But Joḥanan was not removed from his priesthood and remained in his office. Behold, from this incident we see clearly that the hand of the statute of the Torah was not strong over the high priests; or else that the halakhah that a murderer, even when standing at the altar, is taken to be put to death and does not complete the service (Sanhedrin 35a) was not founded until after that time, for some reason unknown to us. For had there been such a statute at that time, why did they leave Joḥanan in his priesthood? And here we cannot say that they were forced to it by order of the king and the governor; on the contrary, the governor opposed him and was angry with him, and would have said nothing had the court wished to remove him.{v1_05_13:1} Apart from this story nothing particular has reached us from that time that touches its religious situation especially.{v1_05_13:2} Also of the names of the men of distinction, the members of the Great Assembly, none is known to us except one, namely Simeon the Just, of whom it is said that he was one of the last of the Great Assembly (Avot 1:2). Although we have no reason to cast doubt on the fact that the beginning of this Assembly was immediately after their return from the exile, and that Ezra was one of its men and without doubt its head, as is hinted in the record in the book called by his name, nevertheless we cannot determine clearly and precisely the length of time for which it lasted, because this too is not clearly known to us: who was this Simeon who was one of the last of the Men of the Great Assembly, and at what time did he live and hold his priesthood? According to what comes out for us from the account of the Talmud, Simeon the Just lived in the days of the great conquest in which Alexander conquered all the lands of the Persian kingdom, and among them also the whole land of Syria. For so it is told in the Talmud (*Megillat Ta'anit* 9; Yoma 69a): when Alexander conquered the kingdom of Persia and subdued under his feet all the lands that had been under its rule, he also went up to Jerusalem. The Jews, whose spirit had been faithful to the kings of Persia, feared Alexander's wrath. And as he drew near to the city, they sent messengers to meet him, of the notables of the people and of the priests, and at their head was Simeon the Just, the high priest, clothed in the garments of his priesthood. And when they met Alexander, he got down from his chariot, gave honor to the high priest, and bowed down to him. His officers wondered at this. And the king told them that he did this because the appearance of this old priest awakened in him the memory of a wondrous dream that he had dreamed when he set out for war: in his dream, behold, the likeness of this honored old man was walking at his right hand, leading him to victory and giving him deliverance in all his wars. For this reason the priest found grace and favor before him, and he promised him that he would do no harm to his people but would show it great kindness. And Alexander also fulfilled his promise. When he came to Jerusalem he offered sacrifices in the Temple. And he agreed to give the Jews license to judge their cases according to the statutes of their Torah, and gave them freedom of belief and religion. He granted them a remission of the tax in every seventh year, which is the year of release; and to the words of accusation with which the Kutim [Samaritans] slandered the Jews he paid no attention (Josephus, *Antiquities*, book 12, chapter 2).⚠2 The king asked him to set up the likeness of his image in the Sanctuary, but the priest answered him that this was against the religion of the Jews. But he promised him that he would make him an everlasting memorial among the Jewish people: every male child born to the priests in that year would be called by his name, Alexander. Now this is told in the Talmud of Simeon the Just. But Josephus the Priest tells it so of Jaddua the high priest. This priest Jaddua died not long after the death of Alexander (about the year of the world 3660). After him Onias his son served as priest, and when he too died his son came in his place, and that was Simeon the Just (Josephus, ibid.). And according to this view Simeon the Just ruled in the days of the turmoil and the wars between Alexander's generals who inherited his kingdom after his death. At that time Ptolemy Lagus besieged Jerusalem and took it, and carried off a great captivity from Israel and led them to Egypt. But also at a time later than this there was a high priest who was likewise called Simeon, and to him too the men of his generation gave the surname "the Just"; he was the son of Onias son of the first Simeon. Simeon the Just the Second held his priesthood in the days of Antiochus the Great (about the year of the world 3720). Some students of antiquity think that this Simeon, who was the grandson of the first Simeon, was the Simeon the Just of whom it is said that he was one of the last of the Men of the Great Assembly.{v1_05_13:3} Now we have no clear proof in hand to decide between the views on this matter, and a decision on it is not needed for our purpose. But it is not right for us to turn our eyes away from the state of affairs of the Jews with regard to the government in the time of Alexander, and likewise in the time of Antiochus the Great. From all that has been made known to us in this respect of the time of Alexander, we have seen that from the time the kingdom of Persia came into Alexander's hand their political situation did not grow worse. He promised them not to change anything in their political and religious affairs and to leave them to their customs and their laws, and he also fulfilled his promise; therefore we have seen no compelling reason for the abolition of the Great Assembly at that time. And likewise there is no reason for its abolition in the days of Antiochus the Great, who was a gracious king to Israel. For although in his wars, which he fought with Ptolemy Philopator, the cup of hardships passed over Israel too, these hardships had no lasting effect; for when Antiochus prevailed, he did very well by the Jews and gave them all the privileges their hearts asked. And in the letter he wrote to his friend and general, the existence of "the great council" is mentioned explicitly, and he wrote to him that he grants them freedom to live according to the law of their religion, and that the members of the great council shall be exempt from the poll tax. So how could we say that at that time the Great Assembly was abolished? But it is not so when Ptolemy Lagus came to Jerusalem: then the matter was reversed. He laid the rod of his wickedness on the lot of the Jews and oppressed them with great oppression; therefore without doubt turmoil came in his wake in their internal affairs as well, and this is a great reason for the abolition of the Assembly. And for this reason we may rightly suppose that at that time the Great Assembly came to an end; and since we have seen that in the days of that turmoil Simeon the Just the First was high priest, therefore he too is the Simeon the Just mentioned in the Mishnah, who was one of the last of the Great Assembly.

1.note: Printed 'book 12, chapter 6'; the story of Joḥanan, Jeshua and Bagoas is Antiquities 11.7.1. Kept as printed.

2.note: Printed 'book 12, chapter 2'; Alexander's visit to Jerusalem is Antiquities 11.8.4-6. Kept as printed.

footnotes.en: I cannot hold back from contending with some of the writers of Jewish history who fill their mouths with reproaches against this man and say that in order to flatter the Romans he twisted the truth; they have transgressed the words of our sages, of blessed memory, who said: "Into a well from which you have drunk water, do not throw a clod." Were it not for Josephus, there would be no writer of history in Israel.
